title: Enums, tuples, and indexers (named values and collection-like access)
hook: Not every concept needs its own class. Enums name discrete values, tuples return a quick bundle without a type declaration, and indexers let a type behave like a collection at the call site.

sections.heading: What are enums, tuples, and indexers?

blocks.text: An **enum** (enumeration) is a named set of integer constants — like a dropdown of allowed values. A **tuple** (`(string id, int score)`) is a lightweight struct that groups a few values without declaring a new type. An **indexer** is a parameterized property (`this[key]`) that makes your type look like an array or dictionary.

entries.plainDefinition: A value type with named integer constants. The default underlying type is `int`.
A struct that groups multiple values. Names are compile-time sugar; fields are `Item1`, `Item2`, etc.
entries.example: `(string id, int score)` — returned from a private helper method.

entries.plainDefinition: A property with parameters, accessed with square brackets. Compiles to `get_Item`/`set_Item` methods.
Unpacking a tuple or any type with a `Deconstruct` method into separate variables.

blocks.text: Enums make closed sets readable — message kinds, auth providers, processing states. Tuples are great for private method returns where a full record would be overkill. Indexers wrap dictionaries and lists with a cleaner API. But tuples are a poor public contract (names vanish across assemblies), and enums deserialized from JSON can hold out-of-range numeric values.

blocks.title: When to upgrade from tuple to record
blocks.body: If a return type crosses assembly boundaries or needs validation, declare a `record` (module 05). Tuples are for internal helpers and quick prototyping.

items.title: Enum for closed sets
items.body: Define named constants. Use `[Flags]` for bit combinations. Always handle unknown values in switches.

items.title: Tuple for quick returns
items.body: Return `(type, value)` from private helpers. Deconstruct at the call site with `var (a, b) = method()`.

items.title: Indexer for collection-like types
items.body: Expose `this[key]` on wrapper types. Overload on parameter type when needed.

items.title: Validate external enum values
items.body: Never trust an enum from JSON or a CSV column. Check with `Enum.IsDefined` or a switch with a default case.

blocks.title: Lightweight types in C# vs JS/TS
rows: `enum` — real CLR type with integer backing
TS string unions are often better than numeric enums
Return an object `{ a, b }` or destructure an array
Bracket notation on objects/arrays — no custom indexer syntax

blocks.title: Public APIs returning bare tuples
blocks.body: `(string, string, string)` as a public return type loses meaningful names across assemblies. Use a `record` with named properties instead.

blocks.title: Switching on enum without a default
blocks.body: JSON and databases can store numeric values outside your enum definition. A switch without `_` or `default` silently misbehaves.

interviewTakeaways: Enums are integers with names; out-of-range values exist at runtime.
Tuples are lightweight private returns, not public contracts.
commonPitfalls: Public APIs returning `(string, string, string)` instead of a record.
Switching on enum without a default for unknown numeric values.

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript string unions are often a better model than numeric enums. C# enums are real CLR types; TypeScript enums may emit objects or disappear depending on compiler settings.
JavaScript destructuring works on objects and arrays. C# deconstruction is an opt-in protocol (`Deconstruct`) plus tuple syntax.
